question.text:
Consider the following C program snippet :

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

void main() &
    int i;
    for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        if (fork() == 0) {
            printf("Child Process: i = %d\n", i);
            _exit(0); // Use _exit to immediately terminate the child
        }
    }
    for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
        wait(NULL);
    }
    printf("Parent Process finished.\n");
}


Assuming all $\verb|fork()|$ calls are successful and the parent process executes the $\verb|wait()|$ loop correctly:

What is the total number of new processes created by this program (excluding the initial parent process)?
question.subject: Operating System

question.text:
In a system, there are four types of resources: $\mathbf{R 1}, \mathbf{R 2}, \mathbf{R 3}$, and $\mathbf{R 4}$. Three processes, $P_1, P_2$, and $P_3$ execute concurrently. At the outset, the processes have declared their maximum resource requirements using a matrix named Max as given below. The number of instances of the resources allocated to the various processes at any given state is given by a matrix named Allocation.

Consider a state of the system with the Allocation and Max matrices as shown below, and in which $\mathbf{3}$ instances of $\mathbf{R1}$, $\mathbf{2}$ instances of $\mathbf{R2}$, $\mathbf{2}$ instances of $\mathbf{R3}$, and $\mathbf{1}$ instance of $\mathbf{R4}$ are only resources available (Total available resources).
 

\[
\begin{array}{c c c c}
 & \text{Allocation} & & \text{Max} \\
& \textbf{R1 R2 R3 R4} & & \textbf{R1 R2 R3 R4}\\
P_1 & 0\ 1\ 0\ 0 & P_1 &1\ 3\ 1\ 1 \\
P_2 & 2\ 0\ 1\ 0 & P_2 & 3\ 1\ 2\ 2 \\
P_3 & 0\ 0\ 1\ 1 & P_3 &2\ 0\ 3\ 1
\end{array}
\]


From the perspective of deadlock avoidance, which of the following is/are true?

  1. The system is in a safe state.
     
  2. The system is not in a safe state, but would be safe if one more instance of $\mathrm{R2}$ were available.
     
  3. The system is not in a safe state, and no process can complete its execution.
     
  4. The system is not in a safe state, but would be safe if the available resources were $\textbf{(4, 3, 2, 1)}$.
question.subject: Operating System

question.text: Consider a system with a pool of $\mathbf{20}$ instances of a single resource type. Each process can request a maximum of $\mathbf{5}$ instances. To guarantee that the system will always avoid deadlock, what is the maximum number of processes $(N)$ that the system can support?

question.text:
In a system, there are three types of resources: $\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{Q}$, and $\mathbf{R}$. Four processes, $T_1, T_2, T_3$, and $T_4$ execute concurrently. At the outset, the processes have declared their maximum resource requirements using a matrix named Max as given below. The number of instances of the resources allocated to the various processes at any given state is given by a matrix named Allocation.

Consider a state of the system with the Allocation and Max matrices as shown below, and in which the Total System Resources available are $\mathbf{10}$ instances of P, $\mathbf{7}$ instances of Q, and $\mathbf{8}$ instances of $\mathbf{R}$.
 

\[
\begin{array}{c c c c}
 & \text{Allocation} & & \text{Max} \\
& \textbf{P Q R} & & \textbf{P Q R}\\
T_1 & 0\ 1\ 0 & T_1 & 4\ 2\ 2 \\
T_2 & 2\ 0\ 0 & T_2 & 6\ 1\ 3 \\
T_3 & 3\ 0\ 2 & T_3 & 3\ 0\ 3 \\
T_4 & 2\ 1\ 1 & T_4 & 4\ 3\ 2
\end{array}
\]


From the perspective of deadlock avoidance, which of the following is/are true?

  1. The system is in a safe state, with a possible safe sequence starting with $T2.$
     
  2. The system is not in a safe state because $T4$ needs $T2$'s allocated resources to finish.
     
  3. The system is in a safe state
     
  4. The system is not in a safe state, as no process can complete its execution.
question.subject: Operating System
